clinicalPearls: SPG49 is an autosomal recessive complicated hereditary spastic paraplegia caused by biallelic variants in TECPR2 (tectonin beta-propeller repeat containing 2), a positive regulator of autophagy; it was first delineated in Bukharian Jewish families carrying a founder truncating variant.

The phenotype is distinctive: spastic paraplegia with intellectual disability plus prominent autonomic and respiratory dysfunction, including central and episodic apnoea and hypoventilation with recurrent respiratory infection.
Severe gastro-oesophageal reflux is characteristic and contributes to aspiration and respiratory morbidity, and is a leading cause of death.
Dysmorphic features (short stature, brachycephaly with a rounded face and coarse features) and a chronic cough are often noted.
A sensory and autonomic neuropathy component may be present, so some patients are described within the hereditary sensory and autonomic neuropathy spectrum.
Loss of TECPR2 impairs endoplasmic-reticulum export and autophagosome formation, placing SPG49 within the expanding group of autophagy-related HSPs.
Recognition matters because respiratory monitoring, reflux control and aspiration prevention materially influence survival.
No cure exists; management is multidisciplinary and largely supportive, with particular attention to breathing, swallowing and reflux.
reference.pathophysiology: SPG49 is an autosomal recessive complicated hereditary spastic paraplegia caused by biallelic loss-of-function variants in TECPR2, which encodes tectonin beta-propeller repeat containing protein 2. TECPR2 is a positive regulator of macroautophagy: it interacts with LC3/ATG8-family proteins and with the COPII machinery to support endoplasmic-reticulum export and autophagosome biogenesis, so its loss impairs autophagic flux and disturbs membrane trafficking. Defective autophagy in long central and peripheral axons is thought to drive the corticospinal degeneration underlying the spasticity, while wider neuronal involvement produces intellectual disability, dysautonomia and brainstem respiratory-control dysfunction with central apnoea and hypoventilation. The disorder was first characterised through a founder truncating variant in the Bukharian Jewish population, and it sits within the growing family of autophagy-associated hereditary spastic paraplegias.
additionalDifferentials: SPG52 (AP4S1) and the other AP-4-deficiency HSPs SPG47 (AP4B1), SPG50 (AP4M1) and SPG51 (AP4E1), and SPG45 (NT5C2) - recessive complicated childhood HSPs with intellectual disability
SPG11 (spatacsin) and SPG15 (ZFYVE26) - recessive HSP with cognitive impairment and thin corpus callosum
Hereditary sensory and autonomic neuropathies, given the autonomic and sensory overlap
Congenital central hypoventilation syndrome (PHOX2B) for the apnoea and hypoventilation phenotype
Rett-like and other neurodevelopmental disorders with disordered breathing
Familial dysautonomia, given the dysautonomia with reflux and aspiration
additionalInvestigations: Molecular testing (exome sequencing or HSP panel) for biallelic TECPR2 variants, with targeted founder-variant testing where ancestry is suggestive
Sleep study and respiratory assessment for central apnoea and hypoventilation
Assessment for gastro-oesophageal reflux and aspiration (pH and impedance studies, videofluoroscopic swallow assessment)
MRI of the brain and spine (a thin corpus callosum, cerebellar or nonspecific changes may occur)
Autonomic function testing and nerve conduction studies for the sensory and autonomic neuropathy
Developmental and cognitive assessment with ophthalmology review
redFlags: Episodes of apnoea, cyanosis or hypoventilation - require urgent respiratory and sleep evaluation and monitoring
Recurrent chest infections or aspiration - a major mortality driver; escalate reflux management and airway protection
Failure to thrive with severe reflux
Autonomic crises with temperature or blood-pressure instability
reference.prognosis: SPG49 is a serious multisystem disorder in which respiratory failure from central apnoea and recurrent aspiration is a major cause of early death; severity nonetheless varies, and diligent respiratory and gastrointestinal supportive care can improve outcomes.
pitfalls: Overlooking the respiratory and autonomic features and treating SPG49 as a motor-only HSP.
Missing silent reflux and aspiration as the driver of recurrent pneumonia.
Not offering founder-variant testing where ancestry is suggestive.
Attributing episodic apnoea to seizures without a sleep and respiratory study.
references: Standard clinical neurology and neurogenetics reference texts
Peer-reviewed reviews on the classification and genetics of hereditary spastic paraplegia
Curated hereditary spastic paraplegia gene and phenotype resources
management: Symptomatic antispasticity therapy with baclofen or tizanidine, and botulinum toxin for focal spasticity
Respiratory management of central and episodic apnoea and hypoventilation, including sleep-study-guided noninvasive ventilation, with prompt treatment of recurrent chest infections
Aggressive control of gastro-oesophageal reflux using proton-pump inhibitors and antireflux measures, with consideration of fundoplication to reduce aspiration
Swallowing assessment with modified feeding or gastrostomy feeding to protect the airway
Autonomic dysfunction management alongside developmental and communication support
Genetic counselling for autosomal recessive inheritance, with founder-variant testing in Bukharian Jewish families and carrier testing of relatives
Multidisciplinary paediatric neurology, respiratory, gastroenterology and rehabilitation input, with an escalation plan for respiratory deterioration
